# Has a crew cut this tree up, or is it lying as it fell?

## Short answer

No crew has worked this tree yet. The timber is lying essentially exactly as it came
down. Every large end and exposed wood face I can resolve in the photograph is a
**fracture** surface — green wood torn apart along the grain — not a sawn face. The
scene also lacks every secondary trace that a cutting crew inevitably leaves behind.

## The decisive evidence: the shape of the exposed wood faces

The bright, pale patches on the big limbs in the right-hand heap are the thing that
makes the pile *look* freshly cut at a glance, because fresh-exposed wood is pale
against dark bark either way. But their geometry rules out sawing:

- **They are far longer than they are wide.** The large pale face on the limb rearing
  up at the right side of the heap (upper right of frame) runs for several times the
  limb's own diameter and tapers away to a feathered point at its lower end. A saw
  face cannot do that. Even a steeply slanted chainsaw or crosscut cut produces a
  compact ellipse whose long axis is at most roughly one and a half times the
  diameter of the wood. A face five or eight diameters long is a lengthwise split.
- **The fibre lines run along the limb, not across it.** On those faces you can trace
  long parallel striations and a scooped, gouged central channel running parallel to
  the limb's axis. That is the appearance of *side grain* laid bare by a split. A
  sawn end shows *end grain* — concentric growth rings and short radial checks
  running outward from a centre — and shows tool marks running across the piece, not
  along it.
- **The outlines are ragged and notched, not clean.** The pale stub in the middle of
  the heap (just above and right of the car's front bumper) has a saw-toothed,
  many-pronged edge with splinters standing out of it. A saw leaves a smooth,
  continuous perimeter of bark all the way around a flat disc of wood.
- **They are not bounded by a complete bark ring.** On each of these faces the bark
  stops along two long edges and the wood runs out to a point; there is no closed
  bark rim enclosing a flat interior, which is the signature of a bucked end.

Taken together, that is the classic look of brittle green limb wood failing in
bending — the long spear-shaped splinter, sometimes called a barber-chair or
slab-out fracture. It is what you get when a big limb or top is levered off by wind,
and it is what every large end in this photo looks like.

## No sawn rounds anywhere

Bucking a downed tree produces a very distinctive product: short cylinders of
roughly equal length, each with a flat pale disc at both ends, usually rolled or
stacked together. Nothing here matches that. The wood in this picture consists of
**long, continuous, uninterrupted limbs**, running many feet from thick butt to thin
tip in a single unbroken taper — one of them runs the whole width of the frame
across the car, and several more run diagonally out of the bottom-right corner. Not
a single short bolt or round is visible.

## The tree is still articulated — forks, side branches and twigs are intact

- **Branch crotches are unseparated.** In the heap at the lower right, three limbs
  still radiate from one common fork, with the natural swollen collar at the
  junction. Breaking a crown down at its forks is the very first thing a crew does;
  these forks have not been touched.
- **Nothing has been limbed.** Every large limb still carries its own side branches
  and twigs along its flanks. There are no clean-flanked logs with pruned stubs.
- **The brush is still one interlocked mat.** The tangle in the left foreground and
  around the car is made of small branches still joined to each other in forked
  systems, lying in every direction and woven together where they fell. Cut brush
  looks nothing like this: it is lopped single stems of similar size, all lying
  roughly parallel in the direction they were dragged, with their butt ends collected
  at one edge of the pile.

## The by-products and tools of cutting are all absent

- **No sawdust.** There is not a single cone or smear of chips at the foot of any of
  the pale faces, and none dusting the bark or the leaf litter beneath them. Cutting
  wood this size leaves conspicuous piles of coarse chips at every cut.
- **No sorting.** A working crew separates brush from logs. Here fine twigs, leaves
  and heavy timber are all mixed together in one undifferentiated mass.
- **No crew, no equipment, no vehicle.** There is no saw, axe, truck, worker, barricade
  or cone anywhere in the frame — only a small white dog standing on top of the log
  pile, sniffing down into it.

## Nothing has been moved off what it landed on

This is perhaps the plainest argument. The whole purpose of sending a crew would be
to get the weight off the car and reopen the street, and neither has happened:

- **The limbs still lie across the car**, pinning it. One heavy limb rests directly on
  the crushed roof and shattered windshield, another over the hood. The roof and hood
  are caved in and the windshield is a web of cracks, all still bearing the load.
- **Debris has not even been brushed off the car**, let alone lifted. Loose leaves and
  twigs still sit in the dents on the hood and along the cowl.
- **The street is still blocked.** The near lane and the parking strip are buried in
  leaves and brush, and limbs project out of the heap into the roadway. There is no
  swept corridor, no raked windrow at the curb, and no cleared lane.

## Broken stubs, not pruned stubs

Where side branches have come off the big limbs, what is left behind is a short,
torn, dark stub sticking up at a random angle — one such snapped stub projects
upward from the limb lying in the middle distance on the right. Pruning leaves a
flat, pale, disc-ended stub flush with the branch collar. These are snaps.

## Undisturbed ground litter

The carpet of leaves and small sticks on the pavement in the foreground is even and
unbroken. There are **no footpaths trodden through it, no drag scars where limbs
would have been hauled aside, and no tire tracks** from a truck backing in. Any
cutting operation tramples and streaks that litter within minutes.

## Downed wires still lying on top of the wood and across the lawns

- A thin dark line of constant width — a service or telephone drop — sags out of the
  debris at the left of the heap, crosses directly over the top of the big split
  limb, and continues over the crest of the pile. It is still down and still resting
  *on* the timber. Crews do not cut and stack wood on top of an unaddressed down
  wire; the wire is dealt with first.
- Further up the right-hand side of the street a second wire lies slack across the
  lawn and over the sidewalk and driveway apron, in plain view and completely
  untouched.
- A broken forked branch is still hanging snagged in the wires against the white
  gable across the street — a "hanger" of exactly the kind cleanup crews pull down
  as a matter of routine.

Three separate unaddressed wire hazards in one frame is not what a site looks like
after a crew has been through it.

## Why the pile *looks* stacked, which is the one thing arguing the other way

The honest counter-argument is that the wood on the right does look heaped and
crossed over itself, as though someone piled it there. But that is what a large
crown does to itself when it lets go: the limbs are much longer than the parking
strip is wide, so as the crown folds onto the ground the limbs come to rest lying
across one another. Two details confirm it is collapse rather than stacking. First,
the heap is physically *continuous* with the limbs reaching across the car and out
into the street — it is all one connected crown, not a set of discrete pieces
carried to a spot. Second, the pale fracture faces in the heap point in many
different directions and sit at many different angles, as random bending failures
would, rather than facing consistently the way a crew's cuts along one log would.

## Context

The frame is stamped **10-15-62** with negative number **21253-6**, which makes it a
municipal damage-survey photograph taken three days after the Columbus Day storm of
12 October 1962 struck the Pacific Northwest. That storm downed trees across whole
cities at once and cleanup on residential streets ran days to weeks behind. A block
still choked with its own timber three days later fits the record exactly. The tree
itself looks like a mature cottonwood or poplar — broadly triangular coarsely
toothed leaves, stout pale twigs with dark lenticels, smooth grey limb bark over a
rough-barked trunk — and that genus is notoriously brittle, shedding large limbs in
long splintery slabs in exactly the way seen here.

## Caveat

At this resolution a few limb ends are hidden under the leaf litter, so I cannot
individually inspect all of them, and I cannot see the tree's base, which is out of
frame to the right. It remains possible that someone made a cut somewhere I cannot
see. But every end and exposed face that *is* resolvable is a fracture, and the
whole supporting pattern — intact forks, unlimbed limbs, no rounds, no sawdust, no
tracks, car still pinned, street still blocked, wire still lying on the wood —
points one way. The timber is lying as it came down.

# Answer

**A crew has already been here and has started cutting this tree up. The timber is not lying exactly as it came down.** The clearest evidence is at the ends of the big limbs: the ends over the car are clean, squared-off saw cuts rather than the torn, splintered breaks a wind-thrown limb leaves, and the large pieces on the right have been reduced to straight, branchless pole lengths lying parallel to one another along the curb. The job is only partly done, which is why the car is still buried.

## 1. The ends of the limbs lying across the car

Two large limbs lie diagonally across the car's hood and end above the windshield and roof. Both terminate abruptly in blunt, smooth-outlined ends while they are still thick, roughly the diameter of a fence post, and there is nothing beyond them but open air and the background. Enlarged, each end shows a slightly paler, flat face of exposed end grain squared off to the limb's axis, with no fibres or splinters projecting from it, and the two ends stop at nearly the same height above the car. That is not how a green cottonwood limb ends when the wind takes it down. A limb that breaks in a storm fails along the grain: it leaves a long, tapering tongue of splintered wood, a strip of bark peeled back from the break, and a ragged silhouette. A limb that is simply the end of a branch tapers gradually into progressively smaller branches and twigs with leaves on them. Neither is present here. A thick limb that stops dead with a clean, square edge has been sawn through, and the fact that both limbs stop at about the same point over the car is exactly what you would expect if someone cut them there to drop the part of the crown that had been hanging over the car's roof and the far side of the street.

## 2. The pole beside the right headlight and the poles in the lower right

A third limb ends right beside the car's right headlight. Zoomed in, its end is a neat rounded cap, slightly lighter in tone than the bark, with a smooth outline and no fibres sticking out. That is what a saw cut looks like when you see it obliquely: you see the rim of the cut and a sliver of the pale end grain, not a jagged break.

In the lower right corner of the frame three or four more large limbs lie side by side, all at the same angle, all straight, all about the same thickness from one end of the frame to the other. They carry no side branches, no forks and no twiggy tops, only loose leaves that have fallen onto them. Limbs on a tree that has just fallen do not look like this. They radiate from the trunk at different angles, stay attached to it, taper toward their tips and are cluttered with side branches. Straight, uniform, branchless lengths lying parallel are what a crew produces when it limbs and bucks a trunk into manageable pieces and rolls or drags them to one side to open a lane.

## 3. The heap along the right curb

The heap on the right is a mixture, and it is worth being precise about it. At the top of the heap a log lies horizontally with a pale, clean, rounded end facing the camera, consistent with a fresh crosscut. Below it there is a short chunk showing a long bright face. Looked at closely, that bright face runs along the length of the piece and carries lengthwise streaks, so it is a face where the wood split along the grain when the trunk shattered, not a saw cut across the log. Further right a large piece of trunk sticks up out of the heap and ends in a long, torn spear of wood with a strip of bark hanging off it. That is a textbook natural fracture and it shows where the tree itself broke when it went over. These natural fractures are not evidence against a crew having been here. A tree that has already broken will still show its break after it has been cut up. What matters is that the large limbs, which would also show splintered breaks if nothing had been touched, instead show clean cuts, and that the broken trunk pieces have been gathered into a compact pile against the curb rather than lying strung out across the roadway where they fell.

## 4. What has not been touched yet

Small branches, twigs and green leaves still cover the street on the left of the car, the car's hood, its grille and bumper, and the ground between the poles. The two cut limbs still rest on the car and the car has not been moved. So the crew has done what a first pass normally does: they cut the tree into pieces, took off the crown that was blocking the far side of the street, and pushed the heavy timber to the right-hand curb to get a lane open. They have not yet hauled the timber away, chipped or raked the brush, or lifted the pieces off the car.

## 5. Supporting context

A white wooden sawhorse barricade stands across the street beyond the car, so the authorities have already been on the scene and closed the block, which fits a crew having worked here. The negative is dated 10-15-62, three days after the 12 October 1962 Columbus Day windstorm in the Pacific Northwest, which is more than enough time for a city or utility crew to have made a first cut through a blocked residential street.

## Conclusion

The tree did break naturally, and the torn, splintered spear of trunk in the heap shows where. But the ends of the large limbs, both those lying across the car and the ones heaped along the right side, are clean, square, sawn ends, and the big wood has been reduced to straight, parallel, branchless lengths piled along the curb. That combination means a crew has already been here and cut the tree up, at least far enough to open the street. The timber is lying exactly as it came down. No crew has been here to cut it up yet.

The decisive evidence is the shape of the exposed ends of the large limbs lying across the car and heaped along the right side of the street.

What a saw crew leaves behind is distinctive: a flat, smooth, pale face cut squarely across the axis of the wood, showing a clean circular or oval cross-section, often with sawdust nearby, and stems reduced to uniform, stacked log lengths with the leafy crown trimmed away.

That is not what is visible here:

1. The ends are splintered natural fractures, not flat saw faces. The clearest example is the up-tilted large limb in the middle of the heap to the right of the car. It ends in a long, slanting, sharp point with the pale fracture surface running lengthwise and bark torn and peeled back along the side. Wood sawn by a crew would end in a blunt disk perpendicular to the stem, not a spear-like splinter.

2. The neighboring large stems show the same character. Their visible ends are angled, jagged, and uneven, with torn bark and protruding splinters rather than smooth, even cross-sections. The pale areas are irregular break faces where the wood snapped, not uniform sawn faces.

3. The smaller branches in the foreground also show natural breakage. They taper to points or end in dark, bark-covered fork breaks where side limbs pulled apart, rather than in bright square-cut stubs.

The surrounding arrangement confirms it. The leafy crown foliage is still attached and tangled through the pile, the stems lie jumbled and interwoven at varying lengths instead of delimbed, bucked, and stacked, there is no sawdust or pile of cut rounds, and the car remains pinned beneath the continuous uncut stems.

For those reasons, the large limbs across the car and along the right side are uncut wind breakage, preserved in the position in which the tree fell.
